YOUR TASK: find real defects in `linuxdo-codex.user.js`, primarily in the ported/new code and in the 48 modified lines of existing code. Priorities:
1. JavaScript correctness: TDZ / initialization-order hazards (module-level `const`/`let` used before initialization at runtime), functions called before definition in a way that matters, wrong variable names, missed guards, off-by-one, wrong selectors.
2. Event/listener issues: duplicate listeners, listeners bound to nodes that get re-rendered (leaks or silently dead handlers), keydown handlers fighting each other (Esc handling for settings panel vs stealth keys vs lightbox).
3. State bugs: toggling a setting must actually take effect (settings panel -> applyVisualSettings/applySettings), stale UI after a setting change, boss view state left inconsistent, `bossAuto` flag semantics ("only auto-restore what the sidebar mode itself hid").
4. Mutual-exclusion / ownership logic: `otherThemeActive()` and the `data-cx-owner` ownership guards. Look for paths where the script touches a foreign theme's UI, deletes it, or fails to yield; also paths where the script's own UI is wrongly treated as foreign.
5. Divergence from the v2ex reference semantics: compare each ported feature against `reference/v2ex-codex.user.js` and report anything that behaves differently in a way that looks unintended (e.g. missing guard, missing re-render, missing cleanup).
6. Anything that would break the pre-existing linux.do features (list loading via /latest.json, topic detail via /t/<id>.json, composer, notifications adoption, bookmarks, likes, polls, read tracking, CF-challenge fallback).

METHOD (suggested)
- `git diff --no-index -U6 linuxdo.user.js linuxdo-codex.user.js > %TEMP%\d.diff` then read that diff; also read the surrounding regions of `linuxdo-codex.user.js` for context.
- For each candidate defect, verify by reading the actual code path end-to-end before reporting it. No speculative findings: state the concrete trigger and the concrete wrong outcome.
- Note: `node --check linuxdo-codex.user.js` passes, and a headless-Chrome smoke test (tools/smoke/) passes 70 assertions covering run/stealth/sidebar/thumbnails/settings/yield — so do NOT report anything those already prove works unless you have a specific counterexample.

tools.name: ask_user_question
tools.description: Ask the user a concise question when you need confirmation, a choice, or missing information before proceeding. Send one or more questions, each with a stable id that will be echoed in the answer.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user before continuing.

id.description: Stable id for this question; echoed in the answer.

question.description: The specific question to ask the user.

header.description: Optional short heading for the question, such as "Confirm" or "Choose Mode".

options.description: Optional choices to show the user. If you recommend one, put it first and append "(Recommended)" to that label.

description.description: One sentence explaining the tradeoff or impact.

multi_select.description: Whether the user may select more than one option. Defaults to false.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

tools.name: dsh_backup_create
tools.description: Create a portable single-file snapshot (.tar.zst) of this DSH home for carrying to the other computer. Excludes credentials, caches, node_modules and regenerable plugin assets; includes settings, agent presets, the profile composition, self-authored plugin sources, workspace/session state and attachments. Restoring it is a separate offline step; this tool never writes into the DSH home.

label.description: Optional note stored in the snapshot manifest, e.g. "before refactor".

snapshotDir.description: Override the snapshot directory (default comes from the plugin config).

sessions.description: Include session transcripts and attachments (default true). Set false to drop sessions/ and attachments/ — the archive still carries the fish-pet res/ asset originals, so expect roughly 40 MB rather than a few KB, because those are already-compressed archives that zstd cannot shrink.

tools.name: dsh_backup_diff
tools.description: Compare what is in the DSH home right now against a snapshot, without writing anything: files only local, files only in the snapshot, and files whose content differs. Use this to see how far the two computers have drifted before deciding which direction to sync.

snapshot.description: Snapshot file name, absolute path, or "latest" (default).

tools.name: dsh_backup_inspect
tools.description: Read one snapshot manifest without extracting it: source machine, creation time, per-tier file counts, the absolute workspace paths recorded at pack time (with their session bucket names), what was excluded and why, and any warnings. Set verify=true to also hash every payload entry against the manifest, which reads the whole archive.

snapshot.description: Snapshot file name, absolute path, or "latest" (default).

verify.description: Also verify every payload entry by sha256 (slow: reads the whole archive).

tools.name: dsh_backup_list
tools.description: List snapshots in the snapshot directory, newest first, with source machine, creation time, file count and size. Also lists available undo points.

tools.name: dsh_backup_plan_restore
tools.description: Work out exactly what restoring a snapshot on THIS machine would do, without writing anything: which bundled workspace path maps to which local path, how each session bucket gets renamed, whether workspace UUIDs get merged, and how many files would be overwritten versus created. Also prints the exact offline CLI command to actually perform the restore. Always call this before restoring.

snapshot.description: Snapshot file name, absolute path, or "latest" (default).

map.description: Path mapping overrides as {"workspace title": "local absolute path"}, for workspaces whose path differs between the two machines.

tools.name: dsh_backup_status
tools.description: Show the DSH backup/sync setup on this machine: DSH home, snapshot directory, machine identity, absolute-path mapping for the two machines, and the newest snapshot. Start here before creating or restoring anything.

tools.name: dsh_backup_undo
tools.description: Roll back the most recent restore on this machine (or a named undo point) from the undo copies taken before each file was overwritten: deletes files that restore created and moves the replaced originals back. Refuses to run while a DSH session is active, because the running Host would overwrite the rolled-back state.

point.description: Undo point id (timestamp). Omit or "latest" for the most recent.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this file operation needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of an operation the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Request cancellation of a background agent's current turn by its agent id. The target may be your direct child or a deeper agent created under you. Only the current turn stops: messages already queued for the agent stay parked until a later send_message, agents it started keep running, and the agent itself stays available for follow-ups. This call returns as soon as the stop request is accepted, so the target may keep running briefly; interrupting an agent that already finished is an accepted no-op.

agent_id.description: The agent id of the running agent to interrupt.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List your continuable background subagents by durable id and label. Use it to recall which ones you started, not to poll for completion — you are told when one finishes. Status comes from the live registry: running means the agent is working right now; inactive means no turn is executing, whether the child is loaded or must be resumed. inactive does not describe task completion, success, failure, or waiting for other agents. A `send_message` steers a running child at its nearest step boundary or starts or resumes a turn for an inactive child, and a direct child remains a `send_message` candidate in every status. The snapshot is not a delivery promise — `send_message` performs the authoritative check and may still fail. Children that could not be read are reported as diagnostics only in `descendants` scope. Scope `descendants` walks the whole tree below you in stable pre-order, annotating each entry with its durable direct-parent session id and depth. You may use `send_message` only for depth-1 entries; deeper entries are candidates for `interrupt_agent` only.

scope.description: children (default) lists direct children only; descendants walks the complete tree below you.

tools.name: present
tools.description: Declare selected existing files accessible through the Session filesystem as final deliverables. Use present when the user needs a separate file deliverable, especially Office documents, spreadsheets, and slide decks. Prefer showing results in your final response when that is sufficient; creating or editing a file does not by itself require present. Usually select the 1-2 most important deliverables; include more when needed, but at most 4 files in a single present call. The files must already exist. The user opens the current source files; their contents are not copied or preserved.

path.description: Path of an existing regular file. Relative paths use the Session working directory.

tools.name: pwsh
tools.description: Execute a PowerShell command (`pwsh -Command`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Paths use native Windows form (`C:\...`); read environment variables with `$env:NAME`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$env:DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. On Windows a force-killed command settles as `[exit code: 1]` without a signal marker — treat it as an interruption, not a command failure. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. A foreground command that reaches its timeout is not killed: it moves to the background the same way, returning its job id and the output so far. Under the Windows sandbox, read-only pwsh runs in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode, while workspace-write stays in FullLanguage unless host policy says otherwise. In read-only, prefer cmdlets and core types (`[string]`, `[datetime]`, `[regex]`, `[guid]`); .NET static calls (`[System.IO.*]::`, `[math]::`), `Add-Type`, COM objects, and reflection fail with "only core types" errors. `-f` formatting, property access, and core cmdlets work. In both confined modes, programs cannot open named pipes, so a command that captures another program's output through piped stdio (Node.js `child_process.spawn`/`exec` with the default `stdio: 'pipe'`) fails with EPERM, while `stdio: 'inherit'` and `stdio: 'ignore'` spawns work and PowerShell's own pipelines are unaffected. That EPERM is the documented boundary: do not retry the command another way — escalate the exact command once or restructure it to avoid capturing output. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "Get-Process" → "List running processes".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to a direct continuable child by its agent id. If you are a resident continuable child, you may also target your direct parent. If the target is still working, the message steers its nearest step; if it is inactive, the message starts or resumes a turn. This call returns no answer from the agent — only confirmation that the message was delivered. A failure means the message was NOT delivered.

agent_id.description: The agent id of your direct continuable child, or your direct parent when you are a resident continuable child.

message.description: The message to deliver to the agent.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` steers the child's nearest step while it is running and starts or resumes a turn while it is inactive. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task for the subagent. It does not share this conversation's context, so include everything it needs.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: subagent_fork
tools.description: Delegate a task to a subagent that inherits this conversation: a child agent seeded with all completed turns so far (it does not see the current in-flight turn). Use this when the subtask builds on this conversation's context — a follow-up analysis, a review, a continuation — without consuming this conversation's context for the work itself. You receive its result, not its intermediate steps. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` steers the child's nearest step while it is running and starts or resumes a turn while it is inactive. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The task for the subagent. It already sees this conversation's completed turns, so build on them freely and state only what is new.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: web_fetch
tools.description: Fetch the content of a specific HTTP(S) URL and return it decoded to text.

tools.name: web_search
tools.description: Search the web for current information. Provide 1–4 queries in the required queries array. Returns an optional summary answer and a list of source URLs.

queries.description: Required search queries; accepts 1–4 items and merges their results.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

The workflow's identity rides the `meta` parameter as JSON: required `name` (short kebab-case) and `description` strings, optional `whenToUse` string and `phases` array (`{title, detail?, provider?, model?}`). The `script` parameter is the plain JavaScript body ONLY (NOT TypeScript, and NO `export const meta` statement — meta is a parameter, not code), running with top-level await; end with `return <value>` — the value must be JSON-serializable and is this tool's result.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf — no pattern/format/numeric bounds) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides (either may be provided alone). Anything else (`effort`/`isolation`/`agentType`) is rejected loudly.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. An ordinary stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) throw errors that ALWAYS kill the script — they never dissolve into a per-item `null`.

Constraints: concurrency and total-agent caps apply; no filesystem, network, timers, or Node.js APIs are provided — the agents do the work, the script only coordinates them. The run executes in the foreground by default: this call returns when the whole script finishes. Set `run_in_background: true` for a long run: the call returns a job id immediately, the run keeps orchestrating in the background, and its return value arrives with the job's completion notice (check on it with `job_output`, stop it with `job_kill`).

content.text:
I've got the full diff now and I'm reviewing it for potential defects. The key issue I'm spotting is in how the `sidebarAutoHide` controller gets initialized and started — even when the sidebar mode is disabled, the `createPageLeaveWatcher` is still being created and started, which seems like unnecessary overhead.

Looking deeper, I see that `applyVisualSettings` calls `sidebarAutoHide.refresh()`, but then `setBoss(true)` resets the `bossAuto` flag to false. This creates a race condition: if a user manually triggers boss mode while the sidebar auto-hide is active, the flag gets cleared, which means the auto-hide logic won't properly track what it should restore later.

There's also a potential issue with `syncTitle()` being called during `applyVisualSettings` before the page is fully initialized, and then being called again in multiple places including `renderCodePanel`. I need to trace through where `renderCodePanel` gets invoked at startup to understand if there's duplication or timing issues.

For H5 specifically, the guard checking `if (!cfg("stealth") && bossOn())` looks correct, but I'm noticing that the 15-second polling interval for `syncRail()` also calls `syncBrandName` and `syncTitle`, which might create unnecessary repeated updates. The Esc key handler calls `preventDefault`, which is fine. But there's a listener registration order problem: `bindStealthKeys` registers first to handle settings panel closing, then `bindSettingsKeys` registers, but both are listening for Esc. Since listeners fire in registration order and `bindStealthKeys` calls `closeSettings()` and returns, the second listener might also run and do something unexpected if it checks `settingsOpen()` again. I need to look at the actual `bindSettingsKeys` implementation to see if there's a real conflict here. I need to check the implementation details across the v2ex reference and the actual code to confirm whether BOSS_CLASS is being added to the document element or body, and whether the lightbox selector properly prevents the theme from treating its own UI as foreign. The smoke test indicates this works, so let me verify the actual code. Checking the regex patterns for the caption—forcing `img.loading` opacity to 1 when pending is the right approach. Now looking at `markSmallImages`: the threshold logic uses `&&` to mark images as no-preview if both dimensions are small, which seems intentional, but I need to verify how this marker is used elsewhere.

The real concern is `bindImgPreview`—it's only called once during bootstrap, and the containers `.cx-turn-agent` and `.cx-turn-user-bubble` don't actually exist in the DOM; those are generated by the code panel. The class names suggest this was copied over and may have missed the actual selectors used in this file. I need to trace where these classes are actually applied in the body content to confirm this is a real defect. Also need to check if `activeLightbox` is properly declared and whether there's actually a variable named that in the code. Looking at the `otherThemeActive()` check in the MutationObserver, when the old script's UI appears, the new script yields and stops injecting styles. If the old script's rail gets removed later, the new script should be able to take over again. I need to verify the cleanup logic and mutation observer handling around line 8085-8150 to see how this transition works.

The smoke test `tools/smoke/probe-foreign.js` covers interop scenarios, so I should check what test cases exist there. I'm noticing a difference in how the image selector handles different contexts—v2ex restricts to `.v2cx-cooked img`, while linuxdo's broader selector targets `.cx-turn-agent img`, which also captures images in the LLM-style reply area. I need to check whether linuxdo's structure actually uses `.cx-turn-agent > .cx-cooked` and if there are nested images in the bubble replies.

There's also a potential issue in linuxdo's `markSmallImages` logic where it checks both naturalWidth and naturalHeight for the 300×200 threshold using AND, but doesn't verify that both dimensions are non-zero—unlike v2ex. This could incorrectly mark zero-dimension images as noPreview. Let me trace through the v2ex implementation around lines 5014-5200 to see how `bindStealthKeys` and `createSidebarAutoHide` handle this.

The bigger concern is that `applyVisualSettings` calls `syncTitle` unconditionally across multiple functions and on a 15-second interval, which could interfere with the native Ember app's title updates — though it looks like it's just re-writing the same string without breaking anything.

I'm noticing a potential issue with the text input handler at line 7871 — it updates `SETTINGS` and calls `applyVisualSettings()` on every keystroke, but the problem is that `SETTINGS[key]` gets set as a string value rather than preserving the original type. When a numeric field like `thumbWidth` comes through as a string, it gets concatenated into the CSS value instead of being converted, which could break the styling.

Looking at the specific settings — `brandName` and `projectName` are text fields, so string values are fine there. But I should verify what `setCfg` actually does, since the diff didn't show changes to it. Let me trace through the `setCfg` implementation to see if it's handling type coercion properly.

There's also a timing concern with the Escape key handling — `bindStealthKeys` runs first, then `bindSettingsKeys`, so the first listener closes the settings panel and prevents the second one from doing anything. That's actually working as intended.

For the lightbox, there's a potential race: if the settings panel is open and the lightbox is also open, pressing Escape closes the settings panel first, then the next Escape would close the lightbox. But the lightbox has its own keydown listener on the document, so I need to check the priority order there. I need to check how the base script handles this interaction, particularly whether the lightbox key handler calls stopPropagation when the settings modal is open.

I'm spotting a potential cleanup issue in the `removeApp()` function. When it removes the `.codex-main` element on non-supported routes like settings or messages pages, it correctly clears the boss window even if the boss class was active, which is fine. But there's something else—

the boss class gets removed without ensuring the actual `.ldx-boss` node is hidden, which should be okay.

Now I'm looking at a bigger issue with `makeFavicon()`. When `favicon` is set to `"codex"` (the default), it captures the original icon elements in `faviconOriginals`. But if the user switches to `"site"`, `restoreSiteFavicon()` removes the favicon element and then tries to use the stored originals. The problem is that `faviconOriginals` specifically filters out `id === FAVICON_ID` and `!icon.dataset.codexShortcut`, so when restoring, it should handle the cleanup correctly—but I need to trace through what happens to those removed elements and whether the restore logic actually accounts for them. Checking the original implementation in linuxdo.user.js to see how makeFavicon handles the FAVICON_ID element's lifecycle — specifically whether it gets skipped or replaced during the icon update loop.

content.text:
I'm looking at a potential infinite loop in the favicon system where `restoreSiteFavicon()` removes elements while the MutationObserver is watching for changes, but the `faviconApplying` guard flag prevents re-entrant calls during the modification. The observer is already active from the initial setup, so when `makeFavicon()` runs and decides to restore the site favicon, it calls `restoreSiteFavicon()` inside a try-finally block that keeps the flag true throughout the operation.

The real problem emerges when the favicon preference is set to "site" mode: `restoreSiteFavicon()` removes our icon link, but the original site link's href has already been replaced with our data URI. Since we're restoring the original href from what we captured earlier, the observer fires on that attribute change, sees the flag is still true, and skips — but then when the user later switches back to the Codex favicon, the original site link now has the site's href again, so `makeFavicon()` correctly overwrites it. The MutationObserver should handle this without looping.

But there's a subtler issue: the flag guard is supposed to prevent re-entrant calls, yet the observer callback runs asynchronously as a microtask after the synchronous code finishes, so there's no re-entrancy problem there. The real concern is that `faviconOriginals` captures the state of all icon links on first application, including the site's original icon at document-start, which should be correct since the page hasn't fully loaded yet.

However, if Discourse's Ember app later adds or replaces icon links after we've captured them, those new links won't be in our captured state, so restoring would leave some links pointing to our icon while others point elsewhere. Also, when we remove the `id` attribute from site icons, that's irreversible and could break Discourse's favicon update logic which looks for specific IDs like `dynamic-favicon`.

Now I need to examine the boss view implementation and the sidebar auto-hide initialization — specifically whether `createSidebarAutoHide` is only called after initialization.

I'm spotting a critical bug in the `renderCodePanel` function: it calls `renderBoss()` when the code panel is visible, but `renderBoss()` completely rebuilds the boss window's code section using `innerHTML`, which destroys and recreates the DOM elements each time the panel re-renders.

Since `renderCodePanel` has a signature guard that prevents re-rendering the same code language and mode combination, the boss window should stay stable during normal navigation. But there's a potential issue if `renderBoss()` is called while the boss window is already active — it would still trigger the rebuild.

I'm also noticing that `renderBoss()` calls `getCodeLang()` and uses the code language system, which might have its own constraints or fallback behavior I need to verify. More importantly, there's a real defect I'm tracking down: `syncRail()` polls every 15 seconds and calls `syncBrandName()` and `syncTitle()`, but when `otherThemeActive()` returns true, the sync is skipped. However, `otherThemeActive()` now checks for `.codex-rail, .codex-main` elements without the owner attribute — and after `bootstrap()` yields to avoid conflicts, any owned nodes should already be removed, so this shouldn't cause issues.

But there's a critical case on first run after upgrading from the old linuxdo.user.js: if the old script runs at document-start and adds its own non-owned `.codex-rail`, the new script's `otherThemeActive()` immediately detects it and yields, leaving the old script in control. The mutation observer also short-circuits on this check, so the new script stays yielded even if the old script is later disabled. This is intentional behavior, not a bug.

Now I'm looking at the boss view state — when `bossOn()` is true and the user toggles `codePanel` off via settings, `applyVisualSettings` calls `setCodePanelHidden(...)` which hides the panel, but the boss view remains active since `renderBoss()` only gets called from `renderCodePanel`. So the code panel gets hidden but the boss stays visible, which seems inconsistent.

I'm also noticing that `renderBoss()` is called inside `renderCodePanel` before returning, meaning the boss view re-renders from the code panel. There's a potential issue with `syncTitle()` in v2ex — it returns early when stealth is off, but in linuxdo it actually rewrites the title, and `applyVisualSettings()` gets called on every text input event, so the title updates happen fairly frequently.

One thing I'm catching: the `input` handler modifies `SETTINGS` directly without calling `setCfg`, so it bypasses persistence (which is fine for immediate feedback), but there's a risk that `SETTINGS[key] = r.value` could store a string where a number is expected — though that's not applicable here since the text fields are brandName and projectName.

Now I need to check the `setCfg` function for the sidebar settings and look for a potential dead handler issue with `otherThemeActive()`.

I'm also wondering whether `ensureRail()` uses `.codex-rail[data-cx-owner="..."]` while `syncModeBtn()` and `syncChrome()` query `.codex-rail` without checking ownership — but the ownership guard in `syncRail()` and related functions should cover that.

I'm tracing through the `syncBrandName` function and noticing a potential issue: when it queries for the codex rail element, if it finds a foreign rail without the `[data-brand-name]` attribute, it returns early. But if that foreign rail somehow has that attribute, we'd end up mistakenly updating someone else's brand name.

Let me check the v2ex implementation to see how it handles this. I need to search for the brand name sync function and understand the semantics of `bossAuto` — specifically whether it should be reset at the end of `setBoss(true)` or if there's a race condition where `hide()` sets `bossAuto = true` after the call completes, which could conflict with the manual toggle reset. Continuing to trace through the logic: when `hideSoon` fires, it sets `shown=true`, then `setBoss(true)` runs and resets `bossAuto=false`, followed by `bossAuto=true`. On restore, it checks if we're still in the auto-triggered session and calls `setBoss(false)`. The `hide()` guard prevents re-entry once `shown` is true, and `bossAuto` stays true until something else changes it.

The ordering between `mouseleave` and `mouseenter` on the root element works correctly—entering cancels the leave timer, leaving schedules it. In `applyVisualSettings`, if the user turns off stealth mode while in boss view, it declares `bossAuto` before calling `setBoss(false, true)`, which sets `bossAuto=false`. No TDZ issues since the variable is initialized first.

Now checking whether `settingsOpen()` correctly identifies our own modal—it looks for `.cx-modal` which could match a foreign script's modal, potentially blocking auto-hide. That's intentional behavior. But there's a potential issue with `renderSettingsPanel`: if a foreign script already has a `.cx-modal` element, we'd reuse it and overwrite its innerHTML, destroying their UI. The port didn't add owner checks to the initial query, so this could be a real defect—the script would stomp on another script's settings modal instead of creating its own.

Let me verify this against the rest of the code and check if the v2ex version handles it differently.

content.text:
I'm noticing a key difference in how the two versions handle foreign rail detection. The new version uses a selector with `OWNER_ATTR` to check ownership, but it's missing the fallback in `syncBrandName`, `showView`, `syncCxNewToggle`, `syncChrome`, and `renderCodePanel` — in those cases, the foreign `.codex-rail` is the issue and `syncBrandName` doesn't have an explicit foreign guard like `syncRail` does.

There's a residual risk after `applyTheme()` early-returns when it detects a foreign theme: the old script's consumers like `renderCodePanel` and `syncChrome` are in an early-return region, so they won't execute. However, `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks like `placeImgPreview` might still be pending and could potentially run against a dead `imgPreviewEl` node, though that appears to be null-checked.

The real concern is the async fetch operations in `loadTopic` and `loadList` — if they're still in flight when the foreign theme takes over, their `.then` handlers will continue to execute, and there's no check for `otherThemeActive` inside those callbacks. This could also apply to the base script, so I need to trace through the actual code flow. I'll commandeer a subagent to handle the v2ex parity comparison in the background while I continue with targeted code analysis. I should get it running so I can reference its findings in my final report.

Subagents have depth limits, so I need to handle this myself. Looking at v2ex's `bindStealthKeys` function, it checks `lightboxOpen` only inside the esc2 branch, whereas linuxdo checks `activeLightbox` earlier before the spec check—which is actually more correct since it applies across all specs. The key difference is that linuxdo's order places the `activeLightbox` check before the spec handling logic.

But there's a potential issue with linuxdo's implementation: when the lightbox is open and the user presses Escape with `stealthKey === "esc2"`, the function returns early, letting the lightbox handler run undisturbed. However, `lastEscAt` isn't reset in this path, so a stale timestamp from a previous Esc press could linger. The 450ms window is tight enough that this might cause unexpected behavior if the user closes the lightbox and presses Esc again quickly—the second Esc could immediately toggle the boss view instead of being treated as a fresh press.

There's also a deeper problem: linuxdo's `bindSettingsKeys` and lightbox handler both register keydown listeners on the document in capture phase, and if both fire on the same Escape, they could conflict. The settings handler prevents default and stops propagation, but depending on listener order, the lightbox might still close anyway since its listener was registered first.

The real concern is how `setBoss(false)` behaves differently between versions — v2ex calls `ensureBoss()` unconditionally, but linuxdo checks if the box exists before hiding it, which could leave stale state if the boss element was removed by a theme transition.

When the old script removes `.ldx-boss` and appends it again, the new script's `ensureBoss` reuses the same node since the query selector finds it. There's also an edge case where `setBoss(true)` is called before the document body exists, but `sidebarAutoHide` already guards against that.

But I'm noticing something in the initialization order—`bootstrap()` calls `scheduleApply()` at the end, which triggers `applyTheme()` in the next animation frame, and that's when `applyVisualSettings` tries to access `document.documentElement`.

The key issue is that `applyVisualSettings` runs before `sidebarAutoHide` is initialized, so the assignment happens at line 8161 first, then `scheduleApply()` at 8178 handles the ordering correctly. And `bindSettingsKeys` checks for both Ctrl/Cmd+comma and Escape, but since `bindStealthKeys` is registered first and calls `stopPropagation` on Escape, the settings binding never sees it when both are open—press Escape once and the panel closes, press again and the lightbox closes.

Now I'm looking at what happens when you press Escape twice quickly while a lightbox is open. The first press gets swallowed by the lightbox check and `setBoss` never flips, but the second press happens within the 450ms window, which means `lastEscAt` gets set again and we can enter the double-Esc detection logic. I need to trace through `settingsOpen()` to see if a foreign modal could interfere with the panel state, and verify whether `resetSettings()` properly cleans up the boss state when stealth is re-enabled. There's also a potential issue with `data-cx-owner` attributes on nodes created by the base script — if the base script gets the updated code via userscript auto-update, it would create `.codex-rail` with `data-cx-owner` set, which could affect ownership detection. ks whether the user has both scripts loaded at the same time. The key distinction is that the base script's `document.title` assignment at line 6470 does write the topic title, which could leak the site name even in stealth mode—but that's the intended behavior. The real concern is whether `applyTheme()` gets caught in a loop since it's called by `scheduleApply()` from the MutationObserver, and even though `applyTheme` adds the `ROOT_CLASS` to the document element, the observer only watches for class attribute changes on the html element itself, so there's potential for a circular trigger.

Looking at the `external` mutation filter more closely: when the observer sees an attribute mutation on the html element, it checks if the element matches the codex UI selector. Since the html element doesn't match `.codex-rail` or `.codex-main`, the filter returns true, which means any class change on the html element triggers `scheduleApply()`. This creates a cycle where `applyTheme()` toggles classes (like `codex-light`, `codex-topic-open`), the observer fires, and `applyTheme()` gets called again in a loop. But this is pre-existing behavior from the base script, and the smoke test passes even with `scheduleApply()` using requestAnimationFrame, so it must be stable enough in practice. Setting a class that's already present won't trigger a mutation, so there's no infinite loop there.

Now I'm looking at a stronger candidate: an inconsistency in `applyTheme()` around line 8017 where it tries to remove `.codex-main`, but the removal might not work as intended.

The key differences I'm tracking are in functions like `renderSettingsPanel` that query for `.cx-modal` without an owner guard, `syncBrandName` that queries for `.codex-rail [data-brand-name]`, and `ensureImgPreview` which always references the module-level `imgPreviewEl`. I need to check whether `decorateCooked` is actually calling `markSmallImages` on the cook element itself and whether the selector matches the cooked content properly.

Now I'm looking at a potential timing issue: CSS constrains images to 260x170, and `markSmallImages` checks `img.complete` and `naturalWidth`. The critical insight is that `markSmallImages` gets called from `decorateCooked` for every post, and the initial guard `if (img.dataset.sized === "1") return` prevents duplicate processing. Since `decorateCooked` is called repeatedly, images could be marked before they're fully in the DOM, but the `dataset.sized` flag should prevent rechecking once marked. The `fullImageUrl` function uses `img.currentSrc || img.src`, which for Discourse lazy-loaded images gives the actual loaded URL, not just a placeholder. I'm also verifying that `hideImgPreview` being bound to `window.addEventListener("scroll", hideImgPreview, true)` with capture doesn't cause issues, and checking whether `markSmallImages` is defined before it's used in `decorateCooked`. Now I'm diving into the `decorateCooked` function to trace through the logic.

Linuxdo reads it dynamically each time, which is actually the correct behavior and a deliberate improvement. But there's a real bug in linuxdo where the `keydown` listener is registered in the capture phase on the window object, which could cause issues with how key events are handled. content.text:
I'm looking at the `bindStealthKeys` function where I found a critical issue: the escape key handler for `esc2` mode returns early without clearing the `lastEscAt` timeout when the lightbox or settings panel is open. This means if a user presses Esc to close a modal (which arms the timer), then quickly presses Esc again within the timeout window, it could trigger unexpected behavior since the timeout state persists across different UI contexts.

Now I'm examining the `setBoss` function to understand how the boss mode state is managed, particularly when the boss element is hidden or removed. I'm noticing a potential issue with the `bossAuto` flag persistence — when the sidebar auto-restore is disabled and the user manually exits boss mode via the escape key, the flag gets reset, which then prevents the auto-restore logic from working correctly on the next return cycle. This causes the sidebar to stay hidden even though it should restore based on the `sidebarAutoRestore` setting. The bug only manifests when `sidebarAutoRestore` is enabled, which is the default behavior, so it's a notable issue worth addressing.

Now I'm shifting focus to the settings panel to check for similar state management issues, particularly around the modal ownership and which configurations are actually read and applied.

Looking at the `renderSettingsPanel` function, I see it retrieves an existing `.cx-modal` element without checking ownership — if a foreign script created one, it gets reused and its innerHTML overwritten, which is a real cross-script interaction bug in the H31 handler. The reset flow in `bindSettingsPanel` has a similar issue where it calls `renderSettingsPanel()` and then `syncSettingControls()` after a reset.

Now I'm checking the thumbWidth preview behavior — when the range input fires, it updates the CSS variable, but I need to verify whether the image thumbnails actually respect this change when the setting is committed. The `markSmallImages` function is called from `decorateCooked` on incremental updates, and there's a potential issue with attached images: if an image loads before `markSmallImages` checks it, the image won't be marked as sized, and the `load` event listener won't fire again, leaving it unprocessed.

But wait — there's a subtle bug here. When `markSmallImages` adds a one-time load listener to a small image that's still loading, the image eventually loads and gets marked as noPreview. But for larger images, the listener fires, the condition fails, and the image never gets marked. The problem is if `markSmallImages` runs again on that same image, both `img.dataset.sized === "1"` and `img.complete` are true, so it gets marked correctly the second time. So the behavior self-corrects on the second pass.

The real remaining concern is the `thumbPreview` toggle — when disabled, `showImgPreview` returns early. It's a solid implementation overall. I should also verify the `esc2` and `lastEscAt` interaction with the lightbox — that's a genuine bug I can confirm. And I need to check the `sidebarAutoHide` variable at line 219 against the v2ex reference to see if their initialization order differs, since the port seems to have introduced a guard not present in the original.

The `.cx-turn-user-bubble` and `.cx-turn-agent` containers exist, so the image selector matches correctly. I'm checking whether emojis are excluded properly—they have the `.emoji` class in the cooked HTML, so emoji images won't be included in the selector. Now I'm verifying the behavior of `markSmallImages` on images within the baked HTML.

There's a subtle issue: images inside `.cx-turn-user-bubble` are marked with `data-no-preview` using a ≤300×200 threshold, but there's a race condition because the lazy-loading attribute was just added. When `img.complete` is true, the dimensions are already known, but if the image hasn't loaded yet, the listener waits for the load event before marking it—which is fine, just delayed.

The click handler in `decorateCooked` opens the lightbox even for images marked with `data-no-preview`, which is acceptable. Now I'm checking the `openLightbox` function—it calls `hideImgPreview()` and `closeLightbox()`, and there's a potential leak with the window mousemove/mouseup listeners that were added in the base. But more importantly, there's a real layout difference: the CSS now sets images to `display:block; width:auto; max-width:var(--ldx-thumb-w)`, which changes how images behave inside paragraphs—they were previously inline, not block-level. I'm checking the boss view state consistency — if the code panel gets disabled while the boss view is active, `renderBoss` doesn't get called, but the boss view persists until Esc or user action, which is acceptable. Now I'm looking at the favicon feature, which writes to `document.title`, and the image preview element is properly owned with the correct attributes. There's a potential issue in `removeApp` where it sets `imgPreviewEl = null` without clearing related state.

The concern is a race condition: if `removeApp` runs while an image is still loading, the load listener might fire after the element is removed, but `hideImgPreview` nulls out the target first, so the listener properly bails out. However, if the boss view exits and `hideImgPreview` runs, it only removes the "on" class rather than fully cleaning up — so the large image remains with `visibility:hidden` via CSS until the next hover, which is fine for preserving the cached image.

Now I need to verify the `esc2` lightbox bug more carefully against the actual code paths.

When the user presses Escape with the lightbox open and stealth mode set to esc2, the event handler returns early without resetting the last-escape timestamp. Then when they press Escape again within 450ms after closing the lightbox, the timestamp check fails and triggers `setBoss` instead — but this shouldn't happen because the lightbox closes on the first press, so a second press would be treated as a fresh keypress rather than a double-press. I'm seeing the issue now—when the smoke test exits via the manual Esc² press at line 200, that triggers `setBoss(false)` which resets `bossAuto = false`, but the test doesn't actually verify that state. The smoke test itself validates the feature works, but there's a gap in the assertion coverage after that exit point.

The real defect is that after manually exiting an auto-hide session with Esc or Ctrl+Shift+H, the next auto-hide cycle won't restore because the flag gets cleared. I need to trace through whether `shown` is still true when the manual exit happens, since `restore()` checks `if (!shown) return;`—but I should verify if `restore()` was even called and what state it left things in. So the bug is confirmed: the auto-hide fires, the user returns (which clears the `shown` flag), then they manually exit with Esc, then leave again—that second auto-hide won't restore because `bossAuto` got reset to false. This is a medium-severity issue that directly contradicts the documented behavior in the settings hint, and the smoke test doesn't catch it because it doesn't cover this sequence.

Now I'm checking whether `syncTitle()` and `syncBrandName()` are properly called in `renderSettingsPanel` after a settings reset. The `setCfg` flow goes through `applySettings` → `applyVisualSettings` → `syncTitle`, so that's covered. For the duplicate-listener concern, `bindRailClicks` uses a `clickBound` dataset flag to prevent double-binding when `ensureRail` recreates. And `bindMainEvents` is called both in `ensureMain` and in a few other places, which could be a problem if the main element gets replaced without the flag being reset.

The `bindMainEvents` function is properly guarded with the dataset check to avoid duplicate bindings. Now I'm reviewing my findings and investigating a few more potential issues—specifically looking at how `applyTheme()` handles the `.codex-main` removal and whether it respects ownership checks, plus examining the boss render condition at line 6533.

I'm also checking the early return logic in `renderCodePanel` around line 6498—if the signature matches and the body already has content, it skips re-rendering, which means if the boss mode was enabled externally while the panel was active, `renderBoss` won't fire again. But looking at the flow, the boss box is created once and stays hidden, so this shouldn't cause issues.

Now I'm verifying the specific claims: whether `lastEscAt` is only reset at line 7579 and never cleared when settings or lightbox close, confirming the variable assignments in the sidebar auto-hide logic, and tracing through the defect scenario where manual boss toggle, mouse leave, and mouse return interact with the `bossAuto` flag—the sequence shows that after a manual toggle sets `bossAuto = false`, a subsequent mouse leave and return restores the system because `bossAuto` is still true from the earlier state.

There's also a second scenario where the user toggles `sidebarAutoRestore` off and back on, then leaves and returns, which triggers the same defect. I'm also considering whether to report the `lastEscAt` staleness issue since it's demonstrable but minor, and then I need to check the `markSmallImages` case where images in the codex/agent selectors lack proper size guards.

Looking at the edge cases more carefully: `hideImgPreview` during boss rendering is fine, the favicon restoration on `applyTheme` is actually correct, but there's a potential issue with `bootstrap()` calling `applyVisualSettings()` before `sidebarAutoHide` is initialized — the assignment happens later at line 8161, so the visual settings get applied first.

Now I need to trace whether `decorateCooked` gets called before `showImgPreview` is defined. The function that calls `decorateCooked` is defined later in the file, but module initialization happens top-to-bottom synchronously, so the function declarations are all hoisted before any code runs. The only top-level call is `bootstrap()` at the end, so there's no TDZ hazard there.

Let me check if there's any other top-level `const` or `let` that could be accessed before initialization — `SETTINGS` is initialized to null and `loadSettings()` runs when `cfg()` is first called. The real concern is whether any module-level constants are referenced during initialization, like in `RAW_CSS` or `buildCss`, but I need to verify if those are defined before `bootstrap` executes.

Now I'm looking at whether `SETTING_CSS_VAR` is actually used in `previewSetting` which gets called at runtime, so that should be fine. Let me also double-check `sidebarAutoHide` and `imgPreviewEl` — both are initialized before their usage points. I'll run a quick verification on the remaining suspicious items, particularly around the `faviconObserver` and the `MutationObserver` that watches head changes. The observer could trigger an infinite loop if `makeFavicon()` keeps re-applying the same attributes, but the guards prevent that — mutations are ignored when `faviconApplying` is true, and once the attributes stabilize, subsequent calls become no-ops. There's a potential issue though when the favicon preference is set to "site": `restoreSiteFavicon()` removes the link elements while the observer is watching...

Since `faviconApplying` is true during that removal, the observer callback returns early and sets `faviconOriginals` to null, so if the site re-adds icons later, they won't be intercepted. The `makeCodexFaviconUri()` cache keyed on `FAVICON_MODE` also handles null returns correctly from the restore path. Let me do a final check on the remaining code one more time.
